project-a.title: Big Love
project-a.body: A focused prop-design case study showing how research, fabrication, finish, and performer needs are translated into objects that feel specific to the production.

sections.image_alt: Cat sitting across a computer keyboard
sections.body: Every prop begins by answering a dramatic question. References establish period and tone, while scale, construction, and handling are planned around the action the performer actually has to repeat.

sections.image_alt: Rubber ducks wearing sunglasses and bright red lips
sections.body: Paint and texture are judged under theatrical light, where a subtle surface may disappear and a glossy one may flare. Final adjustments keep the object believable inside the full stage picture.

project-b.title: The Servant of Two Masters
project-b.body: This project follows the path from visual research to stage-ready prop, balancing character, comedy, durability, and clarity from every seat in the house.

sections.image_alt: Vintage-styled dog dressed like a person reading a letter
sections.body: The finish is developed for the audience view rather than the worktable. Strong shapes, controlled contrast, and intentional wear help the object stay legible without pulling focus from the performer.

sections.image_alt: Cat paw resting dramatically on a computer mouse
sections.body: When a prop carries a joke, consistency matters. Openings, closures, handles, weight, and placement are refined so physical business lands cleanly every time.

project-e.title: BIG LOVE
project-e.body: A compact look at the design thinking behind the objects onstage: what they communicate, how they move, and why the smallest material decision can change a scene.

sections.image_alt: Laptop displaying code beside a lucky cat statue
sections.body: Stage objects are handled again and again. Construction choices prioritize safety, balance, reset speed, and repairability so the prop can support the performance throughout the run.

sections.image_alt: Dog sitting beside a person working at a computer
sections.body: Distressing is most convincing when it suggests specific use rather than generic age. Scratches, patina, repairs, and finish are placed to imply who owned the object and how they lived with it.

project-f.title: Twelfth Night
project-f.body: Prop work lives where storytelling meets practical engineering. This case study traces the choices that make an object readable, usable, and believable under stage light.

sections.image_alt: Tiny kitten peeking over a glowing computer keyboard
sections.body: Paint and texture are judged under theatrical light, where a subtle surface may disappear and a glossy one may flare. Final adjustments keep the object believable inside the full stage picture.

sections.image_alt: Dog wearing round sunglasses with complete confidence
sections.body: A small shift in proportion can make an object elegant, awkward, comic, or threatening. Scale is tested against the performer and surrounding scenery before the design is finalized.
